specPoints.text: understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their reactions with: water; dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid
practical: investigate reactions between dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids and metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc and iron)

primer.text: From Reactivity Series you know that some metals attack dilute acids to give hydrogen while others barely respond. This note turns that idea into a laboratory method: three metals are dropped into two acids, the gas is tested with a lighted splint, and the speed of each reaction ranks the metals in order.

lessons.title: Practical: Investigate Metals reacting with acids
sourceHeadings: Practical: Investigate Metals reacting with acids
lessons.opening: This practical investigates the reactions between dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids and the metals magnesium, iron and zinc. Equal volumes of acid go into three test tubes, a small piece of each metal is added, and any gas given off is tested with a lighted splint. Safety glasses are worn throughout because the acids are being handled directly.
keyPoints: Five cm3 of dilute acid is measured into each of three test tubes.
A length of magnesium ribbon, iron filings and zinc turnings go into separate tubes.
Any gas given off is tested with a lighted splint.
The whole experiment is repeated using dilute sulfuric acid.
Safety glasses are put on before any acid is handled.

low.restatement: Equal volumes of two dilute acids are placed in test tubes and a different metal goes into each. Fizzing means a gas is forming, and a lighted splint confirms which gas it is.
low.analogy: It is like timing three runners over the same track: the track is the same, so any difference in speed belongs to the runners.
low.examPointer: Method questions reward order: name the volumes, the metals, the gas test and the repeat with the second acid.

medium.restatement: The controlled volume of acid and the similar amount of metal keep the comparison fair, so any difference in bubbling reflects the metal alone. A lighted splint that gives a pop identifies hydrogen, and the vigour of each reaction orders the three metals.
medium.analogy: Think of a fair taste test: same cups and same drink volume, so the only thing that can change the verdict is what you add to each cup.
medium.examPointer: Fair-test language earns marks: state what is kept the same, what is changed and what is recorded before quoting the pop test.

check.stem: Why are safety glasses worn during this practical?

options.text: Because dilute acids are being handled directly
options.explanation: The method starts with putting on safety glasses before the acids are poured or the metals are added.

options.text: Because the metals are radioactive
options.explanation: Magnesium, iron and zinc are ordinary metals; the hazard being managed is contact with the acids.
options.misconception: invented hazard substituted for the real one

options.text: Because the lighted splint could ignite the whole tube
options.explanation: The pop test is a small, controlled test; the standing reason for glasses is handling the acids themselves.
options.misconception: single step blamed for the general precaution

options.text: Because the products are always poisonous gases
options.explanation: The gas produced in positive tests is hydrogen; the glasses guard against acid splashes, not poison.

check.stem: What does a lighted splint test for, and what result is expected here?

options.text: Hydrogen, which makes the splint go pop
options.explanation: A lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a distinctive pop when hydrogen is present.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, which turns the splint brighter
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is the gas that extinguishes a lit splint and is tested with limewater, not with a pop.
options.misconception: gas tests crossed between hydrogen and carbon dioxide

options.text: Oxygen, which dissolves the metal
options.explanation: Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and it is not the product of these acid-metal reactions.
options.misconception: wrong gas and wrong observation combined

options.text: Steam, which condenses on the tube wall
options.explanation: Condensation may be seen but it is not what the splint tests; the pop identifies hydrogen.
options.misconception: physical sign confused with the chemical test

check.stem: How much dilute acid is added to each test tube at the start?

options.text: About 5 cm3, measured with a small measuring cylinder
options.explanation: The method specifies a measured 5 cm3 of dilute acid in each of the three tubes.

options.text: The tubes are filled to the brim
options.explanation: Filling to the brim would make fizzing overflow and gives no controlled volume to compare.

options.text: One drop of acid in each tube
options.explanation: A single drop would barely react; the method uses a measured few cubic centimetres.

options.text: The volume varies so that each metal gets a fairer amount
options.explanation: Fairness comes from keeping the volume the same for every metal, not from varying it.

check.stem: Which three metals are investigated in this practical?

options.text: Magnesium, iron and zinc
options.explanation: These are exactly the metals named in the aim and added one per tube.

options.text: Magnesium, copper and silver
options.explanation: Copper and silver are unreactive with dilute acids and are not part of this investigation.

options.text: Sodium, potassium and calcium
options.explanation: These extremely reactive metals are far too dangerous to drop into acids in a school practical.

options.text: Iron, gold and lead
options.explanation: Gold does not react with dilute acids at all and was not one of the three test metals.

check.stem: Why is the experiment repeated with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.text: To see whether the same reactivity pattern appears with a different acid
options.explanation: The repeat lets the ranking be checked against a second acid rather than relying on one set of tubes.

options.text: To make the results more accurate by averaging two pop tests
options.explanation: This is a new comparison, not a repeat for averaging; the acids are different substances.
options.misconception: repeat for precision confused with a new comparison

options.text: Because hydrochloric acid alone cannot react with metals
options.explanation: Hydrochloric acid reacts readily with all three metals; the repeat simply adds the second acid.
options.misconception: false claim about the first acid

options.text: To use up the leftover metal pieces
options.explanation: Nothing in the method depends on leftovers; the repeat is part of the planned comparison.

lessons.title: Results and conclusion
lessons.opening: The results show magnesium dissolving quickly with rapid bubbling and heat, zinc reacting steadily, and iron giving only slow bubbles, with the same story in both acids. Ranking the vigour of the reactions places the metals as Mg > Zn > Fe. In every positive reaction the products are hydrogen gas and a solution of the metal salt.
keyPoints: Magnesium reacts fastest: it dissolves quickly, gets hot and gives a gas that pops with a lighted splint.
Iron is the slowest of the three, showing only very slow bubbling.
Ranking the vigour of their reactions places the metals as Mg > Zn > Fe.
Each metal behaves the same towards both acids, so the pattern does not depend on the acid.
The reactions produce hydrogen gas together with a metal salt in solution.

low.restatement: Faster fizzing means a more reactive metal, so the results order the metals as magnesium, then zinc, then iron. Every positive test gives hydrogen plus a salt dissolved in the solution.
low.analogy: Like ranking sprinters from race times: nobody argues with the stopwatch, and here the bubbles act as the stopwatch.
low.examPointer: Learn the pattern acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen, and be ready to rank metals straight from a results table.

medium.restatement: The vigour of each reaction is the evidence: magnesium reacts with rapid bubbling and heat, zinc responds steadily, and iron is barely visible in its slowness. Both acids give the same ordering, and each reaction yields hydrogen gas with the metal salt left in solution.
medium.analogy: Treat each metal as a runner on the same acid track; the differing speeds, not the track, set the finishing order.
medium.examPointer: The equations in the table are exam staples: magnesium plus sulfuric acid gives magnesium sulfate and hydrogen, so link each observation to its equation.

check.stem: Which metal reacted the most vigorously with the dilute acids?

options.text: Magnesium, which dissolved quickly, got hot and gave rapid bubbling
options.explanation: Magnesium shows the most dramatic signs of reaction in both acids, marking it as the most reactive of the three.

options.text: Iron, because it lasted longest in the acid
options.explanation: Lingering longest shows slowness, not vigour; iron is the least reactive of the three.

options.text: Zinc, because it made the loudest pop
options.explanation: The pop only identifies hydrogen; the pace of dissolving and bubbling is what ranks the metals.
options.misconception: test outcome confused with reaction rate

options.text: All three reacted equally
options.explanation: The table clearly separates fast magnesium, steady zinc and slow iron.

check.stem: Which products form when any of these metals reacts with a dilute acid?

options.text: A metal salt and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Every positive reaction leaves a metal salt in solution and gives off hydrogen, which pops with a splint.

options.text: A metal salt and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide comes from carbonate reactions; metals with acids release hydrogen.

options.text: A metal oxide and water only
options.explanation: No water forms in the acid-metal reaction; the gas evolved is hydrogen.

options.text: Pure metal crystals and steam
options.explanation: The metal is consumed, not produced, and the gas identified is hydrogen rather than steam.

check.stem: Which ordering of the three metals is supported by the results?

options.text: Mg > Zn > Fe
options.explanation: Magnesium reacts fastest, zinc next and iron slowest, which fixes this order.

options.text: Fe > Zn > Mg
options.explanation: That order reverses the observations, which show iron bubbling slowest of the three.

options.text: Zn > Mg > Fe
options.explanation: Magnesium clearly outpaces zinc in both acids, so zinc cannot sit above it.

options.text: No ordering is possible from these observations
options.explanation: The differing speeds of reaction are exactly what allow the metals to be ranked.

check.stem: What was observed for iron in dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.text: Very slow bubbling
options.explanation: Iron is the least reactive of the three test metals, so its reaction is only just visible.

options.text: Rapid bubbling with the metal getting hot
options.explanation: That description belongs to magnesium, the most reactive metal in the table.

options.text: A pink colour change in the solution
options.explanation: No colour change is recorded; iron's sign of reaction is slow bubbling.

options.text: No reaction at all with either acid
options.explanation: Iron does react, just slowly; the table records small bubbles rather than nothing.

check.stem: Why do all three metals show the same pattern with both acids?

options.text: Because the vigour of the reaction is set by the metal, not by which dilute acid is used
options.explanation: Both acids attack in the same way, so the metal's own reactivity decides the speed and the ordering.

options.text: Because the two acids are chemically identical
options.explanation: Hydrochloric and sulfuric acids are different substances; they simply react with metals in the same general way.
options.misconception: different acids treated as one substance

options.text: Because the metals were coated so nothing could change
options.explanation: The metals clearly react; the shared pattern comes from the reaction type, not from any coating.

options.text: Because the pop test forces every reaction to look the same
options.explanation: The pop test only identifies the gas; the pattern is visible in the bubbling before any test.
options.misconception: test procedure blamed for the pattern

glossary.definition: The ranking of metals in order of how readily they react, worked out from reactions with water and dilute acids.
An acid mixed with a large amount of water, used here as hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
A burning wooden splint used to test for hydrogen, which makes it give a pop sound.
The gas released when a reactive metal reacts with a dilute acid.
The compound formed when the metal replaces the hydrogen of the acid, left dissolved in the solution.

workedExample.prompt: In the metals-with-acids practical, magnesium ribbon, iron filings and zinc turnings are added to separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. a) State the observation for each metal. b) Write the balanced equation for magnesium with dilute sulfuric acid. c) Rank the three metals by reactivity as the results support.
steps: a) Magnesium dissolves quickly, gets hot and gives a gas that pops with a lighted splint; zinc bubbles steadily and slowly dissolves; iron shows only very slow bubbling.
b) Mg (s) + H2SO4 (aq) → MgSO4 (aq) + H2 (g) — every positive reaction gives a salt solution and hydrogen gas.
c) The vigour of each reaction is the evidence, so the results order the metals as Mg > Zn > Fe.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Mg vigorous (heat, pop), Zn steady fizzing, Fe slow bubbles. b) Mg + H2SO4 → MgSO4 + H2. c) Mg > Zn > Fe.
